beats.say: At twenty-three minutes past one in the morning, an operator presses the button meant to shut a reactor down. Seconds later, it explodes.
How can the off switch make things worse? The answer is hidden in the physics of one unusual reactor.
This is Chernobyl Unit Four, in Soviet Ukraine, on the twenty-sixth of April, nineteen eighty-six.
To see why it failed, we first need to see how a reactor makes heat. Then we follow its last day, minute by minute.
Chapter one. A reactor is a machine for splitting atoms. Its fuel is uranium, and one kind, uranium two thirty-five, splits easily.
When a neutron hits a uranium two thirty-five nucleus, it splits in two. The pieces fly apart, and that motion becomes heat.
Each split also throws out two or three new neutrons. If one of them splits another atom, the reaction keeps itself going.
That is a chain reaction. The art of running a reactor is keeping it balanced, so each split causes exactly one more.
But the new neutrons are fast, and fast neutrons are bad at splitting uranium. They need to be slowed down first.
So the fuel sits inside a moderator, made of light atoms. Neutrons bounce off them again and again, and slow down.
To turn the power down, operators lower control rods. They contain boron, which swallows neutrons.
Rods in, less power. Rods out, more power. The rods are the reactor's steering wheel.
Finally, a coolant, usually water, carries the heat away. The steam spins a turbine, which makes electricity.
Fuel, moderator, control rods and coolant. Every reactor has them. In one Soviet design, they could work against each other.
Chapter two. Chernobyl's reactors were a Soviet type called the R B M K. Each made thirty-two hundred megawatts of heat.
Its core is a huge stack of graphite blocks, about seven metres tall and nearly twelve across. The graphite is the moderator.
Through the graphite run metal tubes holding the fuel. Water is pumped up through them, and boils as it goes.
Here is the key. The water does two jobs. It cools the fuel, and it also absorbs some neutrons.
When water boils into steam, less liquid is left in the tube. Less water absorbs fewer neutrons, so more of them split uranium.
And the graphite keeps slowing neutrons, steam or no steam. So in this reactor, more steam means more power.
Engineers call this a positive void coefficient. The voids are steam bubbles, and they push power up.
More power boils more water, which makes more steam, which makes more power. It is a loop that can feed itself.
At full power, other effects keep this in check. But below about twenty percent power, the steam effect dominates, and the reactor turns unstable.
There was one more flaw, hidden inside the control rods. It decides everything at the end.
Chapter three. On the twenty-fifth of April, Unit Four is due to shut down for maintenance. First, the crew will run a safety test.
If the plant loses outside power, can the spinning turbine keep the cooling pumps running until the backup generators start?
At one in the morning, the crew starts lowering power. By a quarter to four, the reactor is at half power, sixteen hundred megawatts.
Then, at two in the afternoon, the grid controller in Kyiv asks them to wait. The region still needs the electricity.
So the reactor runs at half power for hours, with its emergency core cooling switched off. Investigators later call this a lack of safety culture.
Only at ten past eleven at night does the power reduction continue. The test has slipped into the middle of the night.
And while the reactor waited, something invisible had been building up inside it: xenon.
Xenon one thirty-five forms from the decay of fission products, and it is one of the strongest neutron absorbers there is.
At full power, neutrons burn xenon away as fast as it forms. But when power drops, xenon piles up and chokes the chain reaction.
Chapter four. Just after midnight, power is about seven hundred megawatts. At twenty-eight minutes past, during a switch of control systems, it plunges.
Power falls to about thirty megawatts. The reactor is almost asleep, and the xenon keeps growing.
The test plan calls for seven hundred to one thousand megawatts. To claw power back, the operators pull out rod after rod.
By one o'clock, they hold the reactor at about two hundred megawatts. Far below the plan, and deep in the unstable zone.
The rules said that if the reserve of rods fell to fifteen, the reactor must be shut down. Most rods are now almost fully out.
Calculations after the accident put the reserve at just eight rods. Investigators think the operator probably did not know.
The reactor is on a knife edge. Low power, little control, lots of xenon, and a strong steam effect.
At one twenty-three and four seconds, the test begins. Steam to the turbine is shut off, and it starts to slow down.
Four of the main cooling pumps run on that slowing turbine, so the water flow through the core begins to drop.
Less flow means more boiling. More steam, more power. For about half a minute, nothing looks wrong.
Then, at one twenty-three and forty seconds, the operator presses the emergency shutdown button, A Z five. The rods start moving down.
Chapter five. To understand what happens next, look closely at a single control rod.
Below the boron hangs a graphite section about four and a half metres long, called a displacer. It keeps water out, to make the rod stronger.
But when a rod is fully withdrawn, a column of water one and a quarter metres tall sits below the graphite, at the bottom of the core.
So when the rods start to fall, the first thing to enter the bottom of the core is not boron. It is graphite, pushing that water out.
Water absorbs neutrons, and graphite barely does. So for the first few seconds, the shutdown rods add power at the bottom of the core.
This is the positive scram effect. It had been seen at another plant, Ignalina, in nineteen eighty-three, but the Chernobyl operators did not know.
And the rods are slow. Going all the way in takes about eighteen seconds.
Three seconds after the button, power passes five hundred and thirty megawatts. More heat makes more steam, and the steam pushes power higher.
Fuel channels rupture. The log records severe shocks, and the control rods stop before they reach the bottom.
One assessment puts the surge at about a hundred times full power. Hot fuel meets water, and a steam explosion tears the core apart.
Two or three seconds later, a second explosion follows. The thousand-tonne plate on top of the reactor is thrown partly aside.
Hot graphite meets air and catches fire. The fire burns for about ten days, lifting radioactive material high into the sky.
Chapter six. So what really caused it? The first international report, in nineteen eighty-six, put most of the weight on the operators.
In nineteen ninety-two, the I A E A's safety advisory group looked again, with new evidence, in a report called INSAG seven.
It found a combination: the reactor's physics, the faulty control rods, and a reactor pushed into a state no procedure covered.
Most importantly, it said, the physics made the unstable behaviour possible. But it still called the operators' critical actions most ill judged.
So the R B M K reactors still running were changed. Extra fixed absorbers and richer fuel tame the steam effect.
Operators now keep a reserve of forty-three to forty-eight rods. And new rods no longer leave water at the bottom.
Full insertion went from eighteen seconds to twelve, and a new fast system drives twenty-four extra rods in under two and a half seconds.
A few of these modified reactors still run in Russia today.
Chernobyl did not explode because of one mistake. A hidden design flaw met a night of risky decisions, and the off switch became the trigger.
